children: By Kimberley Kao and Ying Xian Wong
European companies are ramping up investment across Southeast Asia as they hedge against geopolitical risks, a top industry group says.

As global trade tensions and conflicts force businesses to rethink diversification, Southeast Asia has emerged as a "clear winner" for supply-chain realignments away from the U.S. and China, said Chris Humphrey, executive director at the EU-Asean Business Council.

European businesses feel that Southeast Asia offers the best economic opportunity over the next five years, he said. "The region is geographically well-positioned, connectivity is pretty good, [and it has a] pretty young, highly skilled workforce."

Humphrey heads up an industry group backed by the European Commission and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations that advocates for European businesses in Southeast Asia. Its members include Airbus, Adidas and DHL.

European companies investing in Southeast Asia are aiming to reduce over-reliance on the U.S. and China in an increasingly fragmented trade environment. A growing middle class, rising disposable incomes and maturing markets have also made the region more attractive.
Last year, merchandise trade between the EU and Asean reached $318.8 billion, while foreign direct investment into Asean rose to $31.3 billion from $20 billion in 2024.
A survey of 150 business leaders conducted by the council showed that a majority plan to expand trade and capital deployment in Southeast Asia over the next five years.

"[Foreign direct investment] is not slowing down this year. I think it might actually accelerate," Humphrey said, highlighting data centers, semiconductors and high-end manufacturing as likely targets.
Recent deal activity backs that view.

In June, Austria-based AT&S announced plans to invest up to 2.0 billion euros, or about $2.29 billion, to expand its manufacturing site in Kulim, Malaysia. France-based Mistral AI earlier this year announced partnerships to expand operations in Singapore.
Chinese companies have been expanding rapidly in Southeast Asia too, but Humphrey said that isn't creating friction for European firms.
European businesses don't view Chinese counterparts as an obstacle if the market environment is right, he said: "As long as we're competing on a fair and transparent basis, we don't mind."
Regional governments, for their part, are agnostic about where capital comes from, Humphrey added.
As trade deals ramp up, more investment looks set to flow into Southeast Asia.

Earlier this week, the EU announced a trade pact with the Philippines. Talks with Thailand and Malaysia that are expected to conclude by 2027, and the EU has similar deals in place with Singapore and Vietnam.

Welcoming progress in free-trade ties, the council has urged regional economic ministers to pursue a broader regional economic framework that could pave the way toward an Asean-EU Free Trade Agreement.
But a sweeping deal will need to overcome challenges from non-tariff barriers, regulatory fragmentation and illicit trade.
Governments have lost billions in revenue due to illicit trade, Humphrey said, naming gold, tobacco and pharmaceuticals as problematic sectors.
Persistent external risks factor in too, generating uncertainty that affects investment strategies.
"For governments, [the biggest concern] is trying to predict what's going to happen next in the global geopolitical sphere and realm," he said.
